name_en: Purple-Bud Sheng Pu-erh (Zi Ya / Zi Juan)
cultivar: Zi Ya: naturally purple-shooted plants within seed-grown assamica and wild Camellia populations; Zi Juan: a purple-leaved cultivar selected at the Yunnan tea research institute in Menghai in the 1980s
processing: Standard raw pu-erh processing (pan-firing, rolling, sun drying, pressing) applied to purple-pigmented leaf; the anthocyanins that colour the leaf survive into the cup and tint the liquor.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) for the best lots; wild purple buds are picked by sorting purple shoots out of ordinary gardens, so quantities are small.
appearance_dry: Dark purple-black twisted leaves with violet-tinged buds; Zi Juan is uniformly deep purple, Zi Ya is a purple scatter among green leaf.
appearance_liquor: Zi Juan brews a pale violet-grey to lilac liquor that shifts toward purple-blue with a drop of alkaline water; Zi Ya is greenish gold with a faint purple cast.
appearance_wet: Purple-bronze leaves, with the purple fading toward green in Zi Ya and staying dark in Zi Juan.
taste_profile: Zi Juan is noticeably bitter and herbal with a medicinal, almost ink-like edge and a cool sweet finish; wild Zi Ya is milder, with honey, flowers, a sour-fruity tang and a light body; both have an unusual drying texture.

brewing.notes: Rinse once. Go lighter on leaf and a few degrees cooler than for ordinary sheng, because Zi Juan in particular is bitter; porcelain so you can watch the colour. Do not add lemon unless you want to watch the liquor turn pink.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and by type, which matters more than the year: Zi Juan is a planted cultivar sold in volume as cakes, loose leaf and dragon balls, often with health claims about anthocyanins, while 'wild purple bud' (ye sheng zi ya) is sorted by hand from old gardens and sold in small lots at higher prices. Purple sheng is mostly drunk young (1–5 years); mid-aged purple cakes from the 2000s exist and show the bitterness softening into dried fruit, but there is no aged tradition. Supply is roughly 2008–2025 and dry-stored, and the two types are frequently confused or deliberately mislabelled.
description:
Purple pu-erh is two different things wearing one colour. Zi Ya, 'purple bud', is the natural purple shoot that appears here and there in seed-grown Yunnan gardens and on some wild trees, sorted out by hand and processed separately; Zi Juan is a cultivar bred at the Yunnan tea research institute in Menghai from a purple plant found in the 1980s, planted in rows and purple from stem to bud. Both owe the colour to anthocyanins, the same pigments as in red cabbage and blueberries.

Processing is ordinary sheng, and the pigments survive it: Zi Juan maocha is deep purple-black and brews a lilac-grey liquor that turns pink with lemon and blue-violet with alkaline water, a party trick that sells a lot of tea. Zi Ya is less dramatic, a purple scatter in green leaf and a liquor with only a faint cast.

In the cup Zi Juan is bitter, herbal and faintly medicinal, with a cool sweet finish and a drying texture that is unlike ordinary sheng; it is a tea people drink for its oddness or for its supposed health effects more than for comfort. Wild Zi Ya is gentler, with honey, flowers, a sour-fruit tang and a light body, and a few years of age suits it. Both want less leaf and slightly cooler water than normal sheng.

They are sold by spring year and type, as cakes, loose leaf and dragon balls, and the type is the thing to establish: Zi Juan is plentiful and inexpensive, wild purple bud is scarce and dearer, and a cheap 'wild purple bud' is almost certainly Zi Juan. Health claims about anthocyanins are marketing; the pigments are real, the medical promises are not established.

Try a small amount before buying a cake, because purple tea divides people; and brew it in white porcelain, since watching the colour is half the fun.
sources_note: Zi Juan was selected at the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences Tea Research Institute (Menghai) from a purple plant identified in 1985 according to Chinese sources; registration dates vary. Colour-change behaviour with acid/alkali is the normal anthocyanin reaction.
name_ru: Цзы Я / Цзы Цзюань Шэн Пуэр
history:
Purple-bud pu-erh covers two things that are easy to confuse. Zi Ya is the purple shoot that appears naturally among ordinary Yunnan tea plants, while Zi Juan is a selected cultivar from Yunnan tea research in Menghai, and so a recent tea.

The exact selection and registration dates of Zi Juan are given differently from place to place. Selling these teas under their own names, often with health claims about anthocyanins, is a modern development with no long tradition behind it.
